If your Development Director left tomorrow, who would know which grant reports are due in June?

Not in theory. In practice. Whose laptop has the funder portal logins. Whose inbox has the program officer's last email. Whose head holds the unwritten rule that this funder wants narrative before financials.

At a $500K to $10M nonprofit, the grant function often comes down to one person. Sometimes two. The deadline calendar lives where the work happens, which is wherever that one person works.

This is not a software problem first. It is a documentation problem. But software can make the documentation a side effect of the work instead of a separate task that never gets done.

If you are an Executive Director heading into a Monday board meeting with a finance subcommittee question on restricted fund balances, the print-out you want is the Schedule of Activity by Net Asset Class.

Opening balance, additions, releases from restriction, ending balance. Per fund. One page.

Not the full GL. Not the YTD P&L. The schedule.

We decided early that grants and funds had to be separate database entities. Not the same thing with a flag.

A grant is an award. It has a funder, a period of performance, a budget, reporting deadlines, and a closeout date. It is a contract.

A fund is a bucket of restricted dollars. It can be funded by one grant, by multiple grants, by a private gift, or by a board designation. The restriction sits on the fund.

A single program (say, Youth STEM) can pull from a federal pass-through grant, a foundation grant, and a private donor's restricted gift. Three sources, one fund, one set of allowable costs to track.

If you model that as one table with a "type" column, you spend the rest of the product's life writing exceptions. We modeled it as two tables connected by an allocation table. Boring. Correct. Matches FASB ASC 958 and how Sage Intacct does it.

Most CRMs do not separate these because they did not start in fund accounting. That is fine for tracking gifts. It is not fine for closing a federal award.

Picture this: three different versions of the same grant budget at a Development office. One in QuickBooks, one in a Google Sheet, one in the donor CRM. None of them are wrong. They are all incomplete.

The QuickBooks version has the GL detail but no funder reporting categories.

The Sheet has the funder categories but the actuals are a month stale.

The CRM has the award amount and the contact but no spend data at all.

Three systems, one truth split into thirds. The hand-off between Development and Finance happens by copying numbers between tabs. Every quarter. By a person whose actual job is something else.

Single source of truth is not a slogan. It is the moment one number stops needing reconciliation.

Most "audit prep" advice tells you to start in August. That is too late.

The audit binder is not a document you assemble. It is a byproduct of how you ran the year. If your evidence trail only exists when an auditor asks for it, you do not have an evidence trail. You have a scramble.

Here is the inversion. The week-by-week version of audit prep is not 14 frantic weeks before fieldwork. It is 52 quiet weeks that produce a binder as a side effect.

What that looks like in practice:

Each award has a folder with the executed agreement, the approved budget, every amendment, and the board minutes that authorized it. That folder gets touched on day one and never restructured.

Each drawdown gets a memo. One paragraph. Date, amount, period covered, the GL accounts it ties to. Filed in the award folder when the cash hits.

Each personnel allocation gets a certification at the cadence the funder requires. Federal awards under 2 CFR 200.430 require after-the-fact certification that payroll charges reflect actual work. Frequency varies by agency and funding structure. Filed in the award folder, not in HR.

Each sub-recipient sends back a quarterly compliance attestation. Filed in the award folder. Read by someone, not just received.

When fieldwork starts, the binder is already built. The auditor's PBC list is a retrieval task, not a manufacturing task.

This is the difference between organizations that dread audit week and organizations that schedule it like a dental cleaning. The work was done in the months before. May and June are the right months to set it up for the next cycle.

ALN: Assistance Listing Number. The federal program identifier you used to call CFDA.

The number itself did not change when the name did in 2018. 14.218 is still CDBG Entitlement Grants. 93.243 is still SAMHSA's Projects for Assistance in Transition from Homelessness.

If your award letter says CFDA, the funder is using old paperwork. The number is still valid. Match it on assistancelistings.gov to confirm program details before you cite it in a board memo.

Quick check before Monday: do you know your organization's UEI expiration date?

SAM.gov registrations renew every 12 months. If yours lapses in the middle of a draw request, the federal payment system will reject the drawdown. Not delay it. Reject it.

The renewal window opens 60 days before expiration. Missing this surfaces at the worst time: when SAM.gov support is unavailable.

Two minutes on sam.gov this week. Search your entity, note the expiration date, set a calendar reminder for 60 days prior.

Time-restricted contribution: the donor has tied the gift to a future period. You can spend it, but only after the period begins, or only across the period the donor named.

Purpose-restricted contribution: the donor has tied the gift to a specific program or activity. You can spend it any time, but only on the named purpose.

A multi-year pledge that says "for our scholarship program over the next three years" is both. Time and purpose. The release schedule has to satisfy both at once, and the audit trail has to show it.

This is where spreadsheets quietly fail. They release on one axis or the other. Rarely both.

Before: a quarterly board meeting where the grant pipeline slide is rebuilt from scratch every time, and the numbers do not match the finance slide.

After: the same number, pulled from the same place, by both teams. Boring slides. Calmer meetings.

If you have inherited a grant tracker spreadsheet, the four-item weekend check below tells you what shape it is in.

One: the period of performance dates on every active award. Not the calendar year. The actual start and end on the agreement. About a third of teams have at least one wrong.

Five things that catch small nonprofits off guard on their first federal pass-through award.

1. The pass-through entity (the state or county) is your funder for compliance purposes, but the federal rules still apply. You owe 2 CFR 200 even though your check came from the state.

2. Your UEI on SAM.gov has to be active and matching the legal name on the subaward. Mismatch on a single character delays drawdowns.

3. Period of performance starts on the federal award date the prime received, not the date your subaward letter is signed. Pre-award costs are not automatically allowable just because they happened after you signed.

4. The 15% de minimis indirect rate is available if you have never had a negotiated rate. If you ever negotiated one, even for a closed grant, you cannot fall back to de minimis without re-negotiating.

5. FFATA reporting at $30,000 obligated lives with the prime, but the prime will ask you for the data. Have your DUNS-era history, board comp, and primary place of performance ready.

None of this is in the award letter. It is in the federal regulations the award letter incorporates by reference. Saturday is a fine day to read them.

Conditional contribution: a gift that depends on a future event the donor specifies, like a matching threshold or a program milestone. Under FASB ASC 958-605, you do not recognize revenue until the condition is substantially met.

Unconditional contribution: a gift the donor has handed over with no measurable barrier. Recognize on receipt.

Most "restricted vs unrestricted" confusion is actually conditional vs unconditional confusion. Worth checking on a quiet Saturday.

The two questions to answer before you sit down with the binder.

First, what is the cumulative spend against the period-of-performance budget, by category, today? Not last month-end. Today.

Four reports a board member will ask for in any given quarter, ranked by how often they ask:

1. "How are we doing against budget this year?" Operating budget, actual to date, variance by line. Every meeting.

2. "What is the status of our biggest grants?" The top five awards by dollar value, with period of performance dates, percent spent, and any compliance flags. Most meetings.

3. "How is the donor pipeline looking?" Major gift prospects by stage, year-over-year giving comparison, retention rate. Quarterly.

4. "Where do our restricted funds stand?" Net assets with donor restrictions, by purpose, with current balance and release schedule. Annually, plus any time a major restricted gift is anticipated.

SAM.gov UEI registration expires every 12 months. The hard discovery tends to come the week the federal payment fails to clear.

A few things that help:

Set the renewal reminder 60 days out, not 30. Renewals can take longer than they should, and a lapsed UEI freezes drawdowns on every active federal award you hold.

Document who owns the renewal. The Entity Administrator role on SAM is a person, not a shared mailbox. When that person leaves, the org can lose access until it goes through identity verification again.

Save the active registration confirmation as a PDF and attach it to your federal award records. Auditors check it. Pass-through grantors sometimes ask too.

The system is not friendly. The deadlines are not generous. The cost of missing it is real cash flow, not a slap on the wrist.

Pre-award costs: expenses you incur before the federal award's official start date that you want to charge to the grant.

The default rule under 2 CFR 200.458: not allowable.

The exception: 90 days before the start date, only with prior written approval from the awarding agency. Anything earlier needs explicit agency approval as well.

Where this bites mid-sized nonprofits: you got the verbal "you're getting it" call in March. Start date is April 1. You started hiring the program manager March 15. Those two weeks of payroll are not allowable unless you have the prior approval letter on file.

Get the letter. Save the letter. Attach it to the award record so the auditor finds it without asking.

Three places a grant can live simultaneously:

Board-designated is not restricted. Stop calling it that.

Board-designated funds can be undesignated by the same board that designated them. Donor-restricted funds cannot. The distinction shows up on every audited financial statement under FASB ASC 958, and conflating the two is how organizations end up overstating what they can actually free up.

We decided early that grants and funds would be separate entities in our data model.

A grant is the award. The funder, the budget, the period of performance, the reporting cadence.

Three teams in a $4M nonprofit can produce three different answers to a single restricted-fund question. FASB ASC 958 is why those answers diverge: program spend, fund release, and donor recognition each follow different recognition rules.

If you are negotiating your first NICRA, read this before the call.

NICRA is the Negotiated Indirect Cost Rate Agreement. It is the percentage of direct costs you can charge to indirect under federal awards, negotiated with your cognizant agency.

A few things worth knowing before you start.

The 15% de minimis rate is available without negotiation if you have never had a NICRA. It applies to modified total direct costs. For many mid-sized orgs it lands close to what a negotiated rate would.

If you do negotiate, the cognizant agency is usually the federal awarder giving you the most direct funding. They will want a rate proposal, audited financials, and a cost allocation plan.

A higher rate is not the goal. A defensible rate you can document on every award is.

Three reasons restricted-fund tracking breaks in donor CRMs:

One. Restrictions are properties of the gift, not the donor. A single donor can give a restricted gift this year and an unrestricted gift next. CRMs index on the donor first.

Two. Releases from restriction are events, not statuses. When the Youth STEM program spends $4,200 of a $50,000 restricted grant, that is a release event with a date, an amount, and a reference to the underlying expense. Most CRMs have no event model for this.

Three. The schedule of activity is a financial statement disclosure. It needs to roll up by net asset class, by restriction type, and by fund. CRMs report by donor, by campaign, by appeal. Different axes.

This is not a CRM critique. It is a fit observation. The CRM does what it was built to do. Restricted fund accounting is not on that list.

California nonprofits registered with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers file Form RRF-1 every year. For calendar-year filers, the deadline is May 15 — four months and fifteen days after fiscal year end.

Here is how to complete the filing without getting a deficiency notice.

Step 1: Confirm Registry status. Use the Registry Search tool to verify current standing and your CT file number before doing anything else. A lapsed or suspended registration changes the filing path.

Step 2: Calculate gross annual revenue accurately. This figure determines your fee tier and whether the $2 million audit threshold applies. Fees range from $0 for organizations under $25,000 to $1,200 for those above $500 million. The most common fee mistake is using the wrong revenue tier.

Step 3: Engage an auditor now if at or above $2 million. The Nonprofit Integrity Act of 2004 (Government Code Section 12586(e)) requires an audited financial statement prepared by an independent CPA. The audit must be complete before you file. For calendar-year filers already at this point in April, the window is short.

Step 4: Prepare RRF-1 and attach Form 990. The Registry requires the complete federal Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-PF. Organizations filing the 990-N postcard must still provide California-level detail on the RRF-1 itself.

Step 5: Submit with the correct fee. File online through the Registry portal — online filing reduces deficiency notices caused by attachment errors and missing signatures. Mail submissions with a check payable to "Department of Justice."

Note: California's $2 million audit threshold is separate from the federal Single Audit threshold of $1 million in federal expenditures under 2 CFR 200.501. If your organization sits above both, you may face parallel audit obligations — often handled in a single engagement by the same CPA firm.

How to request a no-cost extension on a federal grant. Eight steps.

Step 1: Confirm your award allows an NCE. Review the Notice of Award. Some awards prohibit extensions or cap them at one extension of up to 12 months. Confirm before drafting the request.

Step 2: Confirm an NCE is the right tool. An NCE is for time, not money. If the real problem is insufficient funding, that is a budget supplement request — a different process with much lower approval odds. Be honest about which problem you have.

Step 3: Request at least 30 days before the period end date. Most agencies require 30–60 days minimum. If your grant ends September 30 and you request on September 15, a 30-day processing timeline means the approval arrives October 15 — after expiration. Costs incurred after the end date but before the extension is approved are unallowable.

Step 4: Contact your program officer before submitting. An informal conversation gives you early indication of approval likelihood and guidance on what justification the agency wants to see. Program officers often have preferences not documented in written guidance.

Step 5: Write a specific justification. Name external factors that caused the delay — personnel vacancy, regulatory approval delay, disrupted program delivery — and describe exactly what work remains. Vague justifications ("we need more time") are routinely denied.

Step 6: Prepare a spend-down projection by budget category. Show what funds remain in each line and the expected expenditures during the extension. Unexplained balances in categories with no spending plan raise flags.

Step 7: Submit through the correct channel. HHS uses different portals than NIH eRA Commons, NSF Research.gov, or HUD's IDIS. Confirm the channel with your program officer.

Step 8: After approval, update your grant record immediately. The new period end date shifts the final SF-425 due date (120 days after period end under 2 CFR 200.344), the final programmatic report, and any compliance calendar items tied to the original end date. File the approval letter in the grant file as an amendment to the Notice of Award.

Myth: if a cost is in the grant budget, it is allowable on a federal award.

Under 2 CFR Part 200, every cost charged to a federal grant must pass three separate tests simultaneously. A cost can appear in the approved budget and still be disallowed.

Test 1 — Allowability: the cost must not be explicitly prohibited under 2 CFR 200.420–200.475. Alcoholic beverages (200.423), entertainment (200.438), lobbying (200.450), and fundraising costs (200.442) are never allowable — regardless of what appears in the budget.

Test 2 — Allocability: the grant must have actually benefited from the cost. Charging 100% of a shared cost to one grant when multiple programs benefited is a common allocability error, even when the total amount is small.

Test 3 — Reasonableness: would a prudent person pay this amount for this good or service in the ordinary course of business? Above-market contracted services, procurements without competitive quotes above the micro-purchase threshold, and equipment that exceeds program requirements can produce partial disallowances based on reasonableness alone.

Budget approval does not substitute for any of these three tests. Document each cost on its own merits at the time of the transaction.

A post-closeout cost transfer on a federal grant requires written authorization from the awarding agency before any journal entry is booked.

Myth: a nonprofit on cash-basis books can report to federal agencies the same way it reports internally.

Missing reconciliation worksheets are one of the more reliable indicators of accounting control weaknesses in single audits.

Cash books and federal reporting can coexist. The bridge is documented, repeatable, and auditable.

Booking a pledge write-off as bad debt expense is one of the most common accounting errors in nonprofit finance — and under FASB ASC 958, it is wrong.

The correct entry debits the allowance for uncollectible pledges and credits the pledge receivable. The write-off reduces the contra-asset and eliminates the receivable. It does not create a new expense on the Statement of Activities.

This matters because most accounting staff coming from for-profit environments do exactly the opposite. The for-profit instinct is a debit to bad debt expense — which is not the correct account under ASC 958-605.

The complication is the allowance itself. If the organization set the allowance to zero when the pledge was recorded, the write-off has nowhere to absorb: it becomes a direct charge to contribution revenue, reducing the current period's reported contributions.

Multi-year pledges add a second entry that gets missed: the unamortized present-value discount attributable to the written-off portion must also be eliminated per ASC 958-605-30-6. Leaving the discount in place after the receivable is gone overstates the discount contra-asset.

Auditors testing pledge receivables will sample write-offs and look for: the original pledge documentation, payment history, collection effort evidence, the collectibility assessment memo, and approval at the threshold specified in your policy.

Net assets without donor restrictions is not the same as cash available.

The term replaced "unrestricted net assets" through FASB ASU 2016-14, effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2017. The substance is identical; only the label changed. Using "unrestricted net assets" in an audited financial statement is now an error.

That $250,000 remains within net assets without donor restrictions, disclosed in the footnotes, not moved to a separate net asset class.


FASB ASU 2016-14 added a required liquidity and availability footnote precisely because a $2 million without-restrictions balance may consist largely of fixed assets, vehicles, and long-term receivables. The 2% cap is where concentrated donor bases get hurt. Contributions from any single source that exceed 2% of total five-year support are capped at the 2% level in the public support numerator. Excess counts in the denominator only.


Program service revenue and investment income count in the denominator (total support) but not in the numerator (public support).


Fail both the one-third test and the 10% facts-and-circumstances test for two consecutive years and the IRS reclassifies the organization as a private foundation by operation of law — triggering the 1.39% excise tax under IRC Section 4940, the 5% minimum distribution requirement, and Form 990-PF filing.


About 100,000 private foundations file Form 990-PF annually compared to 1.5 million public charities. The math behind that ratio runs through Schedule A.

Address loan and loan guarantee programs separately on the SEFA.


Federal loans get specialized SEFA treatment under 2 CFR 200.502. The outstanding balance at year-end plus new loans received during the year is typically reportable, not just current-year cash receipts.


This applies to PPP loans, SBA programs, USDA rural development loans, and similar federal lending. Organizations treating these as cash transactions on the SEFA understate program expenditures.


The reportable figure has three components in most cases: prior-year outstanding loan balance carried forward, new principal disbursed during the fiscal year, and any forgiven amounts recognized in the current period.


Consult 2 CFR 200.502 and the auditor before finalizing the schedule. Loan reporting rules vary by program type, and the OMB Compliance Supplement clarifies treatment for the largest federal lending programs each year.

Questioned costs.


Defined at 2 CFR 200.516, a questioned cost is an expenditure flagged during a single audit because it appears unallowable, unsupported, or unreasonable.


Three categories. Unallowable: violates statute, regulation, or terms of the award. Unsupported: missing documentation. Unreasonable: exceeds what a prudent person would incur in similar circumstances.


The reporting threshold is $25,000 per federal program. When questioned costs attributable to a single program exceed that, they are listed in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs.


Two examples that show up frequently. An auditor finds $32,000 in payroll charged to a federal award without time-and-effort documentation — reported as unsupported, exceeds threshold. A nonprofit charges $18,000 in alcohol-related catering to a training grant — unallowable, under threshold, still disclosed.


Questioned costs are not automatic disallowances. The pass-through entity or federal agency makes the final determination. The audit just flags them.

For advance federal awards, interest earned above $500 per year across all awards must be remitted annually to HHS PSC under 2 CFR 200.305(b)(9).


Most mid-sized nonprofits never compute this until the auditor asks.


Steps 5 and 6 of a monthly grant drawdown reconciliation handle it cleanly.


Step 5: calculate interest on advance balances. Pull the average daily cash balance for each advance award, apply the operating account interest rate, accumulate the monthly figure. Twelve clean monthly numbers turn the annual remittance into addition.


Step 6: document variances and reclassifications. If a draw exceeded expenditures, write down whether it was a timing difference, an accrual, or an overdraw requiring return. If expenditures exceeded draws, plan the next draw to close the gap. Every variance gets a written explanation filed with the reconciliation.


Monthly cadence catches errors while they are still fixable. It also makes the quarterly Federal Financial Report a 30-minute task instead of a fire drill.

Program service revenue is not unrelated business income.


This is where mid-sized nonprofits over-file Form 990-T and pay UBIT they do not owe.


Program service revenue is income earned from activities substantially related to the exempt purpose. A health center charging sliding-scale fees is program service revenue. A literacy nonprofit selling workbooks tied to its curriculum is program service revenue.


Earning it does not jeopardize tax-exempt status. The risk only appears when an activity stops being substantially related and starts looking commercial in scope and substance.


Excessive unrelated commercial activity raises private benefit and inurement concerns, which is a separate analysis from whether the revenue itself is taxable.


The practical test: review activities annually against the exempt purpose stated in your determination letter. Document the connection. Keep that memo with the 990 workpapers.

Federal grant closeout is not a single event. It starts 90 days before the period of performance ends and continues for 3 to 7 years after the grant formally closes.


The 90-day mark is for budget-versus-actual review, no-cost extension decisions, and subrecipient closeout planning. The 30-day mark is for equipment review (capitalization threshold $10,000 under 2 CFR 200.313), unspent funds calculation, and the final obligation lock. The final week is for expenditure lock and reconciliation to the dollar against the accounting system.


Post-period, the final SF-425 is due within 120 calendar days for most agencies, 90 days for some HUD programs. The cumulative federal expenditures on that report must match the GL exactly. A discrepancy is an audit finding.


Record retention under 2 CFR 200.334 is 3 years from the date of final expenditure report submission — not from the period end date. USDA and HUD programs commonly require 7 years. Records involved in pending audits, litigation, or claims must be retained until the matter resolves.

A church that receives a USDA Community Food Projects grant cannot spend a single grant dollar on worship services, religious instruction, or staff time supporting religious activities — even if the food pantry runs out of the same building.


Federal funding requires documented separation between grant-funded secular programs and religious activity. That means tracking personnel time by grant-funded versus religious duties, allocating facility costs proportionally, and documenting that grant participants were not required to participate in religious activities. Reconstructed records at audit time do not satisfy the standard.


The data structure most congregations already use makes this harder than it looks. Building Fund, Missions Fund, General Fund, and youth program designations are restricted in the church's internal sense. They are not the same as grant restriction. Commingling a federal award into the General Fund creates Form 990 reporting errors and audit exposure.


There are roughly 380,000 religious congregations in the U.S. with combined annual revenue of $100-$120 billion (Duke National Congregations Study). Faith-based organizations account for about 32% of all U.S. charitable giving (Giving USA 2023). FEMA Public Assistance, USDA Community Food Projects, and historic preservation grants are the most common federal entry points.


The compliance fix is fund separation enforced at the transaction level — not a tag retroactively applied to a journal entry someone already posted to the wrong account.

The Unique Entity Identifier is a 12-character alphanumeric code assigned by SAM.gov. It replaced DUNS effective April 4, 2022.


Without an active UEI and current SAM.gov registration, a federal grant recipient cannot draw funds — even on an award already in flight. SAM.gov registration is valid for 12 months. There is no grace period. A registration that lapses on Tuesday halts payments on Wednesday.


The UEI is not the EIN. The EIN is the IRS tax identifier. The UEI is the SAM.gov procurement and grants identifier. Both are required, both go on federal applications, and they are different numbers stored in different systems.


Domestic activation runs 7 to 14 business days, with IRS verification typically the bottleneck. Renewal reminders go out 60 days before expiration. The recommended practice is to start renewal on the first reminder, not the last one.


Pass-through entities have a separate obligation under 2 CFR 200.332: collect the subrecipient's UEI before executing any sub-award and check the SAM.gov exclusions list. If the subrecipient is not registered, the pass-through cannot legally execute the agreement.


Registration lapses are among the top five administrative reasons OMB cites for delayed grant drawdowns. The fix is calendar discipline, not a software purchase.

Step 4 of responding to a Single Audit finding: draft the Corrective Action Plan with all five required elements under 2 CFR 200.511(c).


The five elements are the finding reference number, the auditee's position (agree or disagree), the specific corrective action, the named responsible party with title, and the target completion date. Vague language like "management will strengthen controls" is not acceptable and produces a follow-up letter from the awarding agency.


Step 5 is committing realistic timelines. Aggressive but achievable — typically 30 to 180 days depending on complexity. A policy update closes in 30. A system implementation may need 180. Missed CAP deadlines become a finding in the next year's audit, which is how organizations end up in repeat-finding territory.


The package is due the earlier of 30 days after the auditor's report or nine months after fiscal year-end, per 2 CFR 200.512(a)(1). The CAP is part of that package and travels with the report to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse at harvester.census.gov.


A strong CAP reads like a project plan, not a compliance document. "The CFO will update the procurement policy by May 31, circulate it with attestations, and present completed attestations to the audit committee at the June meeting" is what auditors and program officers want to see.

Pass-through entity, defined at 2 CFR 200.1: a non-federal entity that receives a federal award and provides a sub-award to a subrecipient that carries out part of the federal program.


Pass-through status is functional, not optional. The moment a recipient issues a sub-award, it becomes a pass-through entity for that portion of the award and inherits the responsibilities under 2 CFR 200.332.


Two examples that show how broad the definition is. A state department of health receives a $5M HHS grant and sub-awards $3M to 12 county health agencies — the state is the pass-through. A nonprofit receives a $1.2M DOL workforce grant and sub-awards $400,000 to a training partner for one program track — the nonprofit is a pass-through for that $400,000.


The 2 CFR 200.332 obligations include classifying every downstream relationship as subrecipient or contractor, performing risk assessments before issuing sub-awards, and monitoring throughout the period of performance. Pass-through amounts also flow onto the SEFA filed with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse.


If your organization writes checks to a partner under a federal grant, you are probably a pass-through entity. The right time to find out is before the agreement is signed.

Steps 5 and 6 of the in-kind contribution valuation workflow are where most organizations create their next audit finding.


Step 5 is the journal entry. Under ASU 2020-07, debit the asset account (food inventory, supplies, property) or the relevant expense account if the goods are consumed in program delivery, and credit contribution revenue with or without donor restrictions depending on intent. Do not net in-kind gifts against expenses. Netting is the most common error and it understates both revenue and program expense on the 990.


Step 6 is the donor acknowledgment letter. IRS rules require written acknowledgment for any contribution of $250 or more. For in-kind gifts, the letter describes the goods or services in enough detail to support the donor's deduction but does not state a value — that is the donor's responsibility to substantiate.


The standard took effect for fiscal years beginning after June 15, 2021. Most organizations updated their journal entries and forgot to update their footnote disclosures. Audit firms catch this in year three.

Myth: interest earned on a federal advance drawdown counts as program income.


Reality: it does not. Program income is governed by 2 CFR 200.307 and means revenue earned by the recipient that is directly generated by activities supported by the federal award. Interest on cash advances is a separate animal handled under 2 CFR 200.305(b)(9), which requires recipients to remit interest above $500 per year to the HHS Program Support Center.


The two get conflated because both involve money sitting in the recipient's bank account that was not in the original budget. They are not the same thing and they get reported on different schedules.


The other place this matters: the additive-versus-deductive treatment election under 2 CFR 200.307. Once made at award time, that election is binding for the life of the award. Most program officers never ask about it until the auditor does, and by then changing it requires retroactive correction.


If your sub-award says nothing about program income treatment, that is itself a finding waiting to happen.

Audit fees for organizations stuck at the 40 percent major-program coverage threshold typically run $8,000 to $20,000 higher per cycle than for comparable low-risk auditees.


The five low-risk criteria under 2 CFR 200.520 are mostly inside management's control: a clean Single Audit two years running, no material weaknesses in internal controls over major programs, no GAGAS qualified opinion, no fraud findings affecting major programs, and timely Federal Audit Clearinghouse submission.


The catch is that you cannot reverse-engineer eligibility at audit time. The two prior fiscal years either qualify or they do not.


The shops that consistently keep low-risk status track the criteria themselves quarter by quarter, the same way they track cash. The shops that lose it find out from the auditor in March.


Per the AICPA Government Audit Quality Center benchmarking work, the additional testing required for non-low-risk auditees is the single largest avoidable line item in most Single Audit engagements.


GrantPipe surfaces low-risk status indicators alongside grant compliance so the criteria do not get rediscovered at fieldwork.

A question for executive directors at $500K-$10M nonprofits: how long does board prep currently take, and how many systems does the staff touch to assemble the packet?

The pattern is consistent. Revenue year-to-date comes from QuickBooks. Pipeline status comes from a CRM or a spreadsheet. Retention metrics come from a different report. Restricted fund balances come from QuickBooks classes if they exist or a spreadsheet if they do not. Compliance deadlines live in Outlook or one staff member's head.

When each number reconciles differently, assembling a packet that holds up under board scrutiny takes a full week. The ED often does it personally because no one else has context across every system.

Mid-sized nonprofits spend an average of 20 to 30 percent of staff time on compliance data entry across at least 12 different reporting systems per the Center for an Urban Future January 2023 research.

Organizations that compress board prep from a week to an afternoon do it the same way: one system holding donor, grant, restricted fund, and compliance data, with reports generated from live data rather than assembled the night before.
